question_blueprint.learning_objective: Explain how London dispersion forces impact boiling point and why they increase with electron cloud size/surface area even in nonpolar substances.
question_blueprint.target_misconception: Nonpolar molecules have no meaningful intermolecular forces, so all nonpolar substances should have similarly low boiling points and branching or chain length should not matter.
question_blueprint.correct_answer_concept: All molecules, including nonpolar ones, experience London dispersion forces; these become stronger with greater polarizability and more effective surface contact, so larger/less branched nonpolar molecules generally have higher boiling points than smaller/more branched ones.
question_blueprint.expected_reasoning: Students should recognize that temporary induced dipoles exist in all molecules. They should compare either chain length or branching among hydrocarbons and infer that increased size or surface area strengthens dispersion forces, requiring more energy for boiling. The correct answer should rest on stronger dispersion in the larger or less branched molecule, not on permanent dipoles.
question_blueprint.question_style_notes: Use a set of alkanes or hydrocarbon isomers to isolate dispersion effects. Ask for the highest boiling point or the best explanation of a boiling-point trend. Include distractors based on 'nonpolar means no IMFs' and 'more branching raises boiling point because it makes molecules bigger'.

last_candidate.question: Among the C5H12 isomers n-pentane, 2-methylbutane, and neopentane, which has the highest boiling point, and why?

options.A: Neopentane, because greater branching makes the molecule bigger and raises its boiling point
options.B: n-Pentane, because its less branched shape allows greater surface contact and stronger London dispersion forces
options.C: All three have the same boiling point because they have the same molar mass
options.D: 2-Methylbutane, because nonpolar molecules have negligible intermolecular forces so shape does not matter

last_candidate.explanation: All three substances are nonpolar, but all molecules experience London dispersion forces. For isomers with the same molar mass, the key difference is shape. The less branched n-pentane has a more extended shape, which allows more surface contact between molecules and therefore stronger dispersion forces. Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, so n-pentane has the highest boiling point. More branching makes molecules more compact, which lowers surface contact and generally lowers boiling point among these isomers.

question_blueprint.learning_objective: Explain how intermolecular forces impact boiling point by comparing substances capable of hydrogen bonding with those that are not.
question_blueprint.target_misconception: Hydrogen bonding is thought to occur whenever a molecule contains hydrogen anywhere in its formula, so students may predict similarly high boiling points for compounds with O atoms even when no O–H, N–H, or F–H bond is present.
question_blueprint.correct_answer_concept: A compound can have a much higher boiling point than a similarly sized comparison molecule if it can hydrogen-bond to itself; merely having an oxygen atom or being polar is not sufficient. Alcohols boil higher than comparable ethers because alcohol molecules form intermolecular O–H···O hydrogen bonds, whereas ethers cannot donate H-bonds to themselves.
question_blueprint.expected_reasoning: Students should compare two similarly sized molecules such as an alcohol and an ether, recognize that both have dispersion forces and some polarity, then identify that only the alcohol has an O–H bond needed for self hydrogen bonding. They should conclude that the extra intermolecular attraction from hydrogen bonding raises the alcohol’s boiling point above that of the ether, even when molar masses are similar.
question_blueprint.question_style_notes: Use a comparison-based stem with two or three named molecules of similar size, including at least one alcohol and one ether. Ask which has the highest boiling point or which explanation best justifies the difference. Make distractors reflect confusion between 'contains oxygen' and 'can hydrogen-bond to itself,' without reusing the exact butanol/diethyl ether/pentane set from completed question 1.

last_candidate.question: Three compounds of comparable molar mass are ethanol, dimethyl ether, and propane. Which statement best explains why ethanol has the highest boiling point?

options.A: Ethanol has the highest boiling point because its molecules can form hydrogen bonds with each other through an O–H bond.
options.B: Dimethyl ether has the highest boiling point because its oxygen atom lets its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other even without an O–H bond.
options.C: Dimethyl ether has the highest boiling point because its polarity alone makes its intermolecular forces stronger than ethanol’s.
options.D: Propane has the highest boiling point because its nonpolar molecules experience stronger attractions than the oxygen-containing compounds of similar mass.

last_candidate.explanation: Ethanol contains an O–H bond, so ethanol molecules can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds to each other. Dimethyl ether contains oxygen and is polar, but it lacks an O–H, N–H, or F–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen-bond to itself in the same way. Propane is nonpolar and has only London dispersion forces. Therefore, ethanol has the strongest overall intermolecular forces and the highest boiling point.

last_candidate.evaluator_feedback: Content: This item is scientifically sound and acceptable as written. For a stronger version, make distractors more parallel and misconception-focused. For example, keep all options in the form 'X has the highest boiling point because Y' and replace weaker absolutes like 'always' with more plausible reasoning errors about polarity or the presence of oxygen being sufficient for self hydrogen bonding. If desired, also tighten the stem wording from 'similar molar mass' to 'comparable molar mass.'; Quality: Keep the stem and key concept, but revise before operational use. Make all options parallel and comparably plausible, ideally with the same syntactic frame (for example, '___ has the higher boiling point because ___'). Replace weak distractor D with a misconception more tightly tied to the target, such as confusing dipole-dipole forces or oxygen presence with self hydrogen bonding. Reduce clueing from absolutes like 'always' and 'any' unless the correct option uses similar strength of language. If item-set diversity matters, consider a different comparison pair than alcohol versus ether, or ask students to explain why an ether cannot hydrogen-bond to itself rather than repeating the standard boiling-point comparison pattern.; Duplicate: Revise to test a meaningfully different IMF concept or misconception rather than another similar-mass alcohol-vs-ether boiling-point comparison. Good options: (1) compare two molecules where both contain oxygen but differ in branching, shape, or net polarity; (2) ask directly about why a molecule like acetone or dimethyl ether cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, without framing it as a boiling-point comparison against an alcohol; (3) test ranking by IMF strength across several compounds; or (4) target a different misconception such as symmetry vs polarity or branching effects on dispersion forces.
